title: Marketing an Eco-Stay Without Greenwashing
excerpt: How eco-stays, farmstays and homestays can describe their sustainability honestly, with specific, verifiable claims in line with India's 2024 greenwashing guidelines.
description: How to market an eco-stay without greenwashing: risky claims, substantiation, and specific, verifiable wording in line with CCPA's 2024 guidelines.
html:
To market an eco-stay without greenwashing, make only specific claims you can prove, such as "we harvest rainwater for all toilets" and avoid vague labels like "eco-friendly" or "carbon neutral" unless you can back them with data. In India, the CCPA's 2024 greenwashing guidelines make this a legal expectation, not just good practice.

Why greenwashing is a real risk for small stays

Greenwashing means making a property or service look more environmentally responsible than it is. For a homestay, farmstay or eco-lodge it rarely starts as deliberate deception. It usually starts with a word on the website that sounded right: "eco-resort", "sustainable luxury", "green retreat", "zero waste". Then a guest arrives, sees single-use plastic bottles in the room or a diesel generator running all night, and the gap between the claim and reality ends up in a review.

That gap now carries regulatory weight as well. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, India's Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) notified the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Greenwashing or Misleading Environmental Claims, 2024 on 15 October 2024. These sit alongside the CCPA's earlier Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, 2022, which apply to advertising in general. This post is a practical guide, not legal advice. If you are unsure about a particular claim, check with a lawyer.

What the 2024 greenwashing guidelines expect

In summary, based on the published guidelines and legal commentary on them, the main expectations are:

  • Generic terms need qualifiers. Words such as "clean", "green", "eco-friendly", "natural", "carbon neutral" and "sustainable" should be used only with accurate, accessible qualifiers and disclosures that explain what they mean.
  • Claims need verifiable evidence. An environmental claim should be backed by evidence you can produce, not an impression.
  • Say what the claim covers. Be clear whether a claim refers to the whole property or one part of it, for example the cottages but not the restaurant.
  • Do not cherry-pick. Highlighting a favourable fact while hiding a relevant adverse one is treated as misleading.
  • Technical terms should be explained in plain language a guest can understand.
  • Specific claims such as "plastic-free", "compostable" or "net zero" are expected to be supported by credible certification or reliable independent verification.
  • Future goals need a plan. Aspirational claims like "we will be carbon neutral by 2030" should be supported by clear, actionable steps.

Claims that are risky for an eco-stay

Risky claimWhy it is riskySafer, specific alternative
"Eco-friendly resort"Vague; implies the whole property has little environmental impact"Our cottages are built from local laterite and run on solar power during the day"
"Carbon neutral stay"Requires measuring emissions and accounting for them credibly"We have replaced diesel with solar for daytime power and are measuring our remaining use"
"Zero waste"Almost no property sends literally nothing to landfill"We compost kitchen waste on site and send dry waste to a local recycler"
"Plastic-free"A single packaged item can make it untrue"No single-use plastic water bottles in rooms; we provide refillable glass bottles"
"100% organic food"Needs certification or traceable sourcing for every ingredient"Vegetables come from our own garden and two farms in the village when in season"
"Sustainable luxury"A feeling, not a factDescribe the actual practices and let guests judge

The pattern is the same each time: replace a label with a fact, and make sure the fact is true across the whole property you are describing.

How to substantiate what you say

Before any environmental claim goes on your website, OTA listing, Instagram or brochure, you should be able to answer "how do you know?" Keep a simple evidence file, physical or in a shared folder, for every claim:

  • Energy: solar installation invoice, panel capacity, electricity bills before and after, generator fuel logs.
  • Water: rainwater tank capacity, borewell or municipal bills, photos of the greywater system.
  • Waste: arrangement with the local recycler or panchayat collection, compost pit photos, a log of what goes out.
  • Food: names of farms you buy from, receipts, what you grow and when.
  • Local employment: number of staff from the nearby area, stated in a way that does not identify individuals without their consent.
  • Certifications: copies of certificates and their validity dates. Only mention a certification you currently hold, and name it exactly.

Update the evidence file when something changes. If the solar inverter fails and you run the generator for a month, your claim about solar power needs to reflect that or be paused.

Writing claims that are specific and verifiable

A useful test for every sentence: could a guest check this during their stay? "We are committed to the environment" cannot be checked. "There are refill stations for drinking water on every floor" can.

A five-step claim check

  1. Is it specific? Names the practice, not a general value.
  2. Is it true everywhere it implies? If only two of six cottages have solar water heaters, say two.
  3. Do we have evidence? It is in the evidence file and current.
  4. Is anything important left out? If you promote rainwater harvesting but fill a swimming pool from a tanker every week, a guest would consider that relevant.
  5. Is the language plain? A guest without technical knowledge understands it.

Run every page of your site, your OTA descriptions on MakeMyTrip, Booking.com and Airbnb, and your Instagram bio through this check. OTA descriptions are often written once and forgotten.

Branding an eco-stay honestly

None of this means you cannot build a brand around sustainability. It means the brand should rest on what you actually do. A property that says "we are a small farmstay trying to reduce our impact; here is what we do and what we are still working on" is more believable than one claiming perfection. Guests who care about sustainability tend to respect that honesty.

  • Lead with the experience (the forest, the farm, the food, the quiet) and support it with specific practices.
  • Call your property what it is: a homestay, farmstay, cottage stay or lodge, rather than an "eco-resort" if that label is hard to support.
  • Publish a short "how we run this place" page with your practices and, where you measure them, the numbers.
  • Say what you have not solved yet, and what you are doing about it, with dates only if you have a real plan.

Turning those practices into guest-facing content is covered in our post on sustainability content for hotels and stays. For positioning more broadly, see brand positioning for resorts and our hospitality page.

Frequently asked questions

Can I still call my property an eco-stay?

You can describe your property in environmental terms, but a generic label like "eco-stay" or "eco-friendly" should come with clear qualifiers explaining what it means, backed by evidence. Many properties find it simpler and more convincing to describe specific practices, such as solar power or composting, rather than relying on the label itself.

Do the CCPA greenwashing guidelines apply to small homestays?

The 2024 guidelines are framed around environmental claims in advertising and apply to those making such claims, and they do not exempt businesses by size in the summary commentary we reviewed. The safe approach for any property is to treat every public environmental claim, including OTA descriptions and Instagram posts, as needing evidence. Take legal advice for specific situations.

What evidence do I need for a "plastic-free" claim?

Specific claims like "plastic-free" are expected to be supported by credible certification or reliable independent verification, along with accessible data. In practice, a narrower claim such as "no single-use plastic bottles in rooms", which you can show directly, is easier to support than "plastic-free property".

Can I mention future sustainability goals?

Yes, if you have a real plan. The guidelines expect aspirational claims to be backed by clear, actionable steps. Instead of "we will be carbon neutral soon", say what you are doing and by when, for example "we are adding solar panels to the restaurant roof this year", and update guests when it happens.

Where to start

Copy every environmental claim from your website, OTA listings and social profiles into one list. Mark each one as specific and proven, specific but unproven, or vague, then rewrite or remove the last two groups. Start an evidence file for the claims you keep.
